# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-2 (Extended v7)

## Setting and Time
- Multiple time periods: French Revolution era; Napoleonic coronation epoch; present day (spring transitioning to late August/early September, England); future wedding (following spring)
- Primary locations: England (Hampstead, Hull, Liverpool, Dunstead/Kelford harbor towns, Suffolk, London, Welbeck Street, Lowestoft, Torton, Kelmere); Secondary locations: San Francisco, New York, Eastern Prussia, Germany, Hamburgh; French locations (D——, Manosque, Sisteron, Hautes-Alpes, Paris, Italy, Durance, Château-Arnoux, Senez, Briançon, Aix, Draguignan)
- Atmospheric details: Rain threatening; wind with salt and tar smell; frosted hedges; smoke lying flat; bees in lavender; dog barking; bell for vespers; children chasing hoop shrieking; gulls over fish heads; cart with turnips; chalk sun on forge wall; road rutted and puddled after thaw; light going early; baker's boy late at oven

## Main Characters and Relationships

**M. Charles Myriel / Monseigneur Bienvenu (Bishop)**
- French aristocrat; family ruined by Revolution; emigrated to Italy at very beginning of Revolution
- Wife died in Italy of chest malady after long suffering; had no children
- Returned from Italy as a priest; became Bishop of D——
- About epoch of coronation, went to Paris on curacy business; encountered Napoleon in anteroom during Emperor's visit to Cardinal Fesch
- Takes up abode in hospital; receives 15,000 francs yearly from State as bishop's salary
- **Redistributes entire salary across 23 charitable categories including Hospital, seminaries, maternity societies, foundlings, orphans, poor teachers, and general relief; retains only 1,000 livres for personal expenses**
- **Subsists on 1,000 livres personal allowance plus 500 francs pension of sister = 1,500 francs yearly**
- **Within less than a year, became treasurer of all benevolence and cashier of all those in distress; considerable sums of money passed through his hands**
- Made no change to his mode of life, added nothing superfluous to bare necessities
- Provoked great outcry among local burgesses through his charitable arrangements
- Known affectionately by poor people as Monseigneur Bienvenu (Welcome)
- **Born Provençal; easily familiarized with dialects of the south; speaks all tongues, enters into all hearts; perfectly at home in thatched cottage and mountains; understands how to say grandest things in most vulgar idioms**
- Does not omit pastoral visits despite converting carriage into alms; visits thirty-two curacies, forty-one vicarships, and two hundred eighty-five auxiliary chapels
- Traveled on ass to Senez when purse very dry; when scandalized mayor questioned, Bishop explained he rode the animal used by Jesus Christ from necessity, not vanity
- Kind and indulgent during pastoral trips; talks rather than preaches; uses examples from neighboring districts to teach
- Conversation gay and affable; puts himself on level with two old women beside him; laughs like schoolboy; relatively short stature
- **Philosophy on flesh and temptation: "Man has upon him his flesh, which is at once his burden and his temptation...He must watch it, check it, repress it, and obey it only at the last extremity. There may be some fault even in this obedience; but the fault thus committed is venial; it is a fall, but a fall on the knees which may terminate in prayer."**
- **Teaches: "Teach those who are ignorant as many things as possible; society is culpable, in that it does not afford instruction gratis; it is responsible for the night which it produces. This soul is full of shadow; sin is therein committed. The guilty one is not the person who has committed the sin, but the person who has created the shadow."**
- **Gentle raillery conceals serious meaning; caught M. Géborand giving a sou to six poor beggar-women on Sundays after hearing sermon on charity, and remarked with smile: "There is M. Géborand purchasing paradise for a sou"**
- When begging for poor in drawing-room, told Marquis de Champtercier (wealthy, avaricious): "You must give me something"; when Marquis claimed he had poor people of his own, Bishop replied "Give them to me"
- Not to be rebuffed even by refusal when question of charity arises
- **Attended condemned murderer's execution; passed entire day with him in prison, forgetful of food and sleep, praying to God for the soul and praying the condemned man for his own. Taught him the best truths; was father, brother, friend; bishop only to bless. Mounted the tumbril and scaffold with him. At the moment when the knife was about to fall, the Bishop said to him: "God raises from the dead him whom man slays; he whom his brothers have rejected finds his Father once more. Pray, believe, enter into life: the Father is there." The sufferer, previously gloomy, became radiant. After descending from the scaffold, there was something in his look which made the people draw aside; they could not tell which was most worthy of admiration, his pallor or his serenity.**
- **On his return home, said to his sister, "I have just officiated pontifically." Afterward appeared crushed; his almost violent serenity had disappeared; the phantom of social justice tormented him. He seemed to be reproaching himself. Subject to lugubrious monologues: "I did not think that it was so monstrous. It is wrong to become absorbed in the divine law to such a degree as not to perceive human law. Death belongs to God alone. By what right do men touch that unknown thing?" He ruminated on the nature of the scaffold as instrument of social justice; considers it not a piece of carpentry but a being possessed of sombre initiative, appearing to see, hear, understand; accomplice of the executioner; devouring, eating flesh, drinking blood.**
- **Daily life: Sleeps little; morning meditation for one hour; says mass at cathedral or house; breaks fast on rye bread dipped in milk of his own cows**
- **As Bishop must daily receive secretary (canon) and nearly daily his vicars-general; reprove congregations, grant privileges, examine ecclesiastical library, write charges, authorize sermons, reconcile curés and mayors, conduct clerical and administrative correspondence**
- **Devotes remaining time to necessitous, sick, afflicted; time remaining from them, he devotes to work—digs in garden, reads, writes. Calls both kinds of toil "gardening," saying "The mind is a garden"**
- **Towards midday when weather fine, takes stroll in country or town, often entering lowly dwellings; walks alone, buried in own thoughts, eyes cast down, supporting himself on long cane, clad in wadded purple garment of silk, wearing purple stockings inside coarse shoes, surmounted by flat hat with three golden tassels of large bullion**
- **His presence has something warming and luminous; children and old people come out to doorsteps for him as for the sun; he bestows blessing and they bless him; they point out his house to any one in need**
- **At half-past eight in evening sups with sister; Madame Magloire serves; repast extremely frugal: ordinary diet consists only of vegetables boiled in water and oil soup. When he has one of his curés to supper, Madame Magloire serves excellent fish from lake or fine game from mountains; every curé furnishes pretext for good meal. Said in town: "when the Bishop does not indulge in the cheer of a curé, he indulges in the cheer of a trappist"**
- **After supper converses for half hour with Mademoiselle Baptistine and Madame Magloire; then retires to own room to write on loose sheets or margins of folios. Man of letters and learned; left behind five or six curious manuscripts including dissertation on Genesis verse "In the beginning, the spirit of God floated upon the waters," comparing three texts (Arabic, Josephus, Chaldaic); examines theological works of Hugo, Bishop of Ptolemaïs**
- **Sometimes in midst of reading falls into profound meditation and writes few lines on pages of volume; these often have no connection with book containing them. Wrote marginal note on volume of American Revolutionary correspondence: "Ecclesiastes calls you the All-powerful; the Maccabees call you the Creator; the Epistle to the Ephesians calls you liberty; Baruch calls you Immensity; the Psalms call you Wisdom and Truth; John calls you Light; the Books of Kings call you Lord; Exodus calls you Providence; Leviticus, Sanctity; Esdras, Justice; the creation calls you God; man calls you Father; but Solomon calls you Compassion, and that is the most beautiful of all your names."**
- **Called to bedside of sick and dying at any hour; understands this is his greatest duty and labor. Widowed and orphaned families need not summon him; he comes of own accord. Knows how to sit and hold peace for long hours beside man who lost wife of his love, mother who lost child. Knows moment for silence and moment for speech. Seeks not to efface sorrow by forgetfulness but to magnify and dignify it by hope. Says to despairing: "Have a care of the manner in which you turn towards the dead. Think not of that which perishes. Gaze steadily. You will perceive the living light of your well-beloved dead in the depths of heaven." Points out resigned man to counsel and calm despairing; transforms grief which gazes upon grave by showing grief which fixes gaze upon star.**
- **Household arrangement: Lives in ground floor of three-room structure with story above; first room serves as dining-room, second is bedroom, third is oratory (no exit except through bedroom; no exit from bedroom except through dining-room). Detached alcove with bed in oratory for visiting country curates. Hospital pharmacy transformed into kitchen and cellar; stable in garden (formerly hospital kitchen) holds two cows; invariably sends half their milk daily to hospital sick people. Furniture extremely sparse and austere: square table in white wood and four straw-seated chairs in winter salon and dining-room; pink painted antique sideboard in dining-room; altar in oratory constructed from similar sideboard with white napery and imitation lace. Still retains six silver knives and forks and soup-ladle from former possessions (formerly ate from silver dishes, now finds it difficult to renounce). Two straw prie-Dieu in oratory; straw armchair in bedroom. Bedchamber: hospital bed of iron with green serge canopy; glazed door opening on garden; bookcase cupboard with glass doors; wooden chimney painted to represent marble (habitually without fire); pair of iron firedogs ornamented with garlanded vases and flutings formerly silvered; copper crucifix with worn-off silver on threadbare velvet background; large table with inkstand and papers; prie-Dieu before bed. Two oval-framed portraits on wall beside bed: Abbé of Chaliot, Bishop of Saint Claude, and Abbé Tourteau, vicar-general of Agde, both appointed by king on April 27, 1785 (found with house, left undisturbed). Antique curtain of coarse woollen stuff at window, so old Madame Magloire had to seam middle (seam forms cross; Bishop calls attention to it delightfully). Red brick paved chambers washed weekly with straw mats before all beds. House exquisitely clean—sole luxury Bishop permits, saying "That takes nothing from the poor." Mademoiselle Baptistine's ambition had been to purchase yellow Utrecht velvet drawing-room furniture with rose pattern and mahogany in swan's neck style with sofa (would cost 500 francs; managed to lay by only 42 francs 10 sous in five years; renounced idea). Large easy-chair of formerly gilded wood covered with flowered pekin in Baptistine's room; had to be hoisted through window as staircase too narrow. Another chair in alcove with half straw gone and three legs, serviceable only propped against wall.**

**Mademoiselle Baptistine** (Bishop's sister)
- Long, pale, thin, gentle creature; embodiment of respectability
- Never was pretty; whole life succession of holy deeds; acquired beauty of goodness; leanness became transparency
- In receipt of yearly income of 500 francs sufficient for personal wants
- **Overheard Bishop's self-reproaching monologues about the scaffold and death; preserved them**
- Subsists on shared 1,500 francs yearly with bishop and their servant
- Occupies first floor with Madame Magloire

**Madame Magloire** (Bishop's servant)
- Only servant in bishop's household
- Grumbled a little about financial arrangement
- Likes to call Bishop "Your Grace"
- Subsists on shared 1,500 francs yearly with bishop and Mademoiselle Baptistine
- Takes advantage of curés visiting to supper to serve Bishop excellent fish and game
- Attends to household cleaning; discovered paintings beneath washed-over paper in Mademoiselle Baptistine's chambers; contemplates silver knives, forks, and soup-ladle with delight daily
- Occupies first floor with Mademoiselle Baptistine

**Mrs. Hurtle** (now Mrs. Fisker, departed)
- American woman, formerly engaged to Mr. Montague
- Forgave him but remained deeply wounded; sacrificed revenge through strategic self-abasement
- Final meeting: threw herself into Montague's arms, declared love "with my very heart of hearts," covered his face with kisses; he responded with cold constraint; she released him with dignity
- Afterward: collapsed prone on floor, then became unusually gracious to Mrs. Pipkin
- Departed Liverpool September 3rd for New York with Marie Melmotte, Madame Melmotte, Hamilton K. Fisker, Herr Croll
- Became Mrs. Fisker very soon after arrival at San Francisco
- Never to revisit England; carries miniature portrait of Mr. Montague into future marriage

**Mr. Montague (Paul)**
- English gentleman; weak regarding women
- Abandoned Mrs. Hurtle upon meeting English girl
- Will marry Marie Melmotte and remain in England
- Soon after Hetta's arrival in Suffolk, came down to Carbury
- Received by Roger with warmth and old manner; Roger kept promise to treat him as though he were his brother
- Roger spoke to Paul much of land, tenants, labourers, own farm, amount of income, and necessity of living so income always sufficient

**Marie Melmotte** (now Mrs. Fisker, departed)
- Young, beautiful daughter of deceased Melmotte
- Concerned about propriety regarding Mrs. Hurtle's reputation; easily swayed in Montague's favor
- Became engaged to Hamilton K. Fisker; understood at Hampstead
- Departed Liverpool September 3rd for New York; became Mrs. Fisker very soon after arrival at San Francisco
- Determined never to revisit England; reminiscences not happy

**Mr. Hamilton K. Fisker** (departed)
- American associate; passionate but grew less wise as bigger
- Fixed departure as September 3rd
- Became engaged to and married Marie Melmotte very soon after arrival at San Francisco

**Madame Melmotte** (departed)
- Widow of deceased Melmotte; mother of Marie
- Recently widowed; engaged to marry Herr Croll; arrangement subject to censorious objections
- Departed Liverpool September 3rd for New York; determined never to revisit England

**Herr Croll** (departed)
- Associate of American establishment; Germanic accent; astute character analyst
- Engaged to and married Madame Melmotte; departed Liverpool September 3rd for New York

**Lady Carbury (now Mrs. Broune)**
- Mother of Sir Felix and Hetta; financially burdened
- Agreed Mr. Broune's proposition: Sir Felix receives £175 per year if travels to Germany; nothing if remains
- Initially rejected Mr. Broune's marriage proposal two or three months ago, chiefly because of son's position
- After Sir Felix's exile confirmed, Mr. Broune renewed proposal; she accepted by kneeling at his feet with face buried on his knees
- Before winter was over, became wife of Mr. Broune; took his name
- That night experienced thorough reaction of spirit; world changed from perfect blank to rose-colored
- Viewed Mr. Broune as one of considerable ones of world; believed being his wife was career enough
- Mrs. Broune's Tuesday evenings much more regarded by literary world than Lady Carbury's
- Knows her son well; gave him five-pound note at parting; Mr. Broune expressed angry energy upon learning this

**Sir Felix Carbury**
- Son of Lady Carbury; brother of Hetta
- Exhausted funds; last sovereign almost gone; no tradesman will give credit; key to door taken; page treats him with contumely; clothes rusty
- Assented to Mr. Broune's proposition to travel to Germany/Eastern Prussia
- Duly introduced to Rev. Septimus Blake
- Spent last sovereign on farewell dinner at Beargarden
- Before end of August, embarked from Hull for Hamburgh with Blake family
- Mother gave him five-pound note at parting

**Mr. Broune**
- Great editor; powerful and influential man
- Proposed marriage to Lady Carbury two or three months ago; she declined chiefly because of her son
- Changed manner toward her; less gentle than before
- Very obstinate, reasonable, somewhat hard of heart
- Persuaded Lady Carbury to allow Sir Felix to travel to Germany; threatened homelessness and financial deprivation if he remained
- Offered £175 per year if Sir Felix went
- Between him and Mr. Blake, ensured Sir Felix's departure from Hull before end of August
- Renewed marriage proposal after her son's exile, saying circumstances changed
- Expressed angry energy upon learning Lady Carbury gave Sir Felix five-pound note at parting
- Accepted by Lady Carbury; married her before winter was over
- Believed he never loved her better than when she refused him, because he thought she did so from propriety
- Became "quite another person"—different from earlier gentle behavior

**Hetta Carbury**
- Daughter of Lady Carbury; sister of Sir Felix
- Does not want her mother's company
- Engaged to marry Roger Carbury; marriage fixed for following spring
- Invited by Mrs. Yeld (Bishop's wife) to stay at palace in Suffolk
- Left London before hearing of her mother's engagement with Mr. Broune
- Will spend autumn and possibly winter in Suffolk to become accustomed to Roger in his new capacity
- After arrival at palace, Roger visited and walked with her in garden for couple of hours two days after the Bishop's conversation

**Roger Carbury**
- Landowner in Suffolk; gentleman with considerable property (Carbury estate)
- Loves Hetta Carbury; she agreed to marry him; wedding set for following spring
- Believed Paul Montague unfit to marry Hetta due to his conduct with Mrs. Hurtle
- Will not tell tales against Montague even when pressed
- Resigned to never marrying or having children of his own
- Conceived idea that Hetta should spend autumn and winter in Suffolk to become accustomed to him
- Induced Mrs. Yeld to invite her down to palace
- Told much of his story to the Bishop (his friend); in consequence Mrs. Yeld invited Hetta
- Bishop discouraged him from settling property on Hetta or her children, warning he might yet marry and citing King Lear
- Abandoned idea of settling property on Montague's children but remained resolute in determination to make himself subordinate to cousin's interests
- Conquered his regrets; now looks forward to Hetta's and Paul's presence at Carbury as source of all future happiness
- Will make Paul welcome as though he were his brother, and Hetta as though she were his daughter
- Resolved that all anger is gone; threw his hands up as though scattering indignation to the air
- Holds property as steward for those to come after him
- Told Hetta she will teach herself to regard him as her best and closest friend
- Assured her Marie will come and enjoy it; that is settled
- Promised after Marie's visit, Carbury will be Hetta's home so she learns to care about and love the place
- Acknowledged Carbury will be Hetta's home really in future; she will be Squire of Carbury when he is gone
- Could not bring himself to say Paul Montague should be Squire of Carbury
- Hopes "all our troubles are over now," referring to himself and Hetta

## Secondary Households
- Stenson household (Torton): Matho and Ismira Stenson; 4 children: Kassa, Orrald, Pelde, Gazek
- Stenworth household (Torton): Havus Stenworth and wife Fewyn Stenworth; 4 children at home: eldest daughter Yera Stenworth; son Lurald Stenworth; son Davus Stenworth; daughter Pelde Stenworth
- Corrley household (Kelmere): Gadan and Zalis Corrley; 3 children: Rinelle, Kadan, Taric
- Thornmere household (Ostcombe): Islan and Vesmira Thornmere; 2 sons: Jotho, Isric
- Stenenridge household (Dunstead harbor town): Rozek Stenenridge and wife Luena Stenenridge; 2 children at home: eldest son Thizek Stenenridge, daughter Pewyn Stenenridge
- Corrford household (Dunstead harbor town): Yedan Corrford married to Nylia Corrford; 3 children in order of birth—eldest son Ulrald Corrford; son Marald Corrford; daughter Yewyn Corrford
- **Ulrald Corrford and Kassa Stenson are husband and wife; couple lives in Dunstead**
- **Marald Corrford and Fenelle Lindmere are husband and wife; couple lives in Dunstead**
- **Gazek Stenson and Pelde Stenworth are husband and wife; couple lives in Torton**

## Other Characters
- The Bishop and Mrs. Yeld: Roger's friend and confidant; prudent wisdom; invited Hetta
- Rev. Septimus Blake: Clergyman; traveled with Sir Felix from Hull to Hamburgh
- M. le Cardinal Fesch: Powerful church figure; Napoleon's uncle
- Napoleon: Emperor; encountered Bishop Myriel
- M. Géborand: Wealthy retired merchant, usurer; amassed two millions in cloth manufacture; never gave alms until after hearing sermon on charity; afterward gave sou to six beggar-women at cathedral door every Sunday
- Marquis de Champtercier: Wealthy, avaricious old man; simultaneously ultra-royalist and ultra-Voltairian

## Key Events
- Sir Felix exiled to Germany/Eastern Prussia before end of August
- Lady Carbury married Mr. Broune before winter was over
- Hetta invited to stay at palace in Suffolk; left before hearing of mother's engagement
- Roger visited Hetta at palace; they walked in garden
- Paul came to Carbury; Roger received him warmly
- September 3rd: Madame Melmotte, Marie, Mrs. Hurtle, Fisker, Herr Croll departed Liverpool for New York
- Marie and Fisker married very soon after arrival at San Francisco
- **Bishop attended condemned murderer's execution and entered deep moral crisis regarding state-sanctioned death**

## Themes
- Religious devotion and charitable duty; practical compassion superseding institutional role
- **The moral weight of state-sanctioned execution; justice versus mercy; conscience and the torment of witnessing institutional violence**
- **Universal human dignity and the divine law transcending human law**
- Redemption through charity
- Resignation and acceptance of life's disappointments
- Property, inheritance, and future generations
- Male honor and keeping promises despite personal pain
- Simplicity and austerity as spiritual practice
- Domestic comfort renounced for charitable purpose
